newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amnesty sought for South Africa church killing.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty sought for South Africa church killing.

text.p: Three former black guerrillas on Wednesday applied for amnesty for one of the bloodiest attacks on civilians in South Africa's race war, the killing of 11 people at a church service.
The application is being opposed by some of the people wounded in the July 1993 attack on St James Church in Cape Town by four members of the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) armed wing.
"I was fighting for political liberation," said one of the four, Bassie Mkhumbuzi, who is on bail after being charged with 11 counts of murder.
He was 17 at the time of the attack, carried out with hand grenades and automatic rifles on a largely white congregation that included some blacks.

Lawyers for the victims opposing the amnesty application, brought before Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, asked Mkhumbuzi why he regarded a church as a legitimate target.
"Most of the white churches were used to oppress blacks," he replied. "I knew they were used by our enemies."
Mkhumbuzi acknowledged that he knew that Tutu, black former head of the predominantly white Church of England, had been a leading anti-apartheid activist.
One of the victims, Russian seaman Dmitry Makogon, said in a letter to the commission that he had lost both legs and an arm in the attack.
"The aim of the commission is to establish the truth...the truth is that the amnesty applicants attacked unarmed and defenceless people," he wrote.
Mkhumbuzi said he would like to meet the Russian to apologise because he now regretted attacking the church.

The commission has powers to grant amnesty to those who committed political, but not racist, crimes during apartheid. The aim is to encourage perpetrators to come forward with the full truth and to promote reconciliation.
The hearing into the St James Church attack, carried out during the final stages of negotiations on South Africa's all-race elections in April 1994, was adjourned until Thursday.
